parole.testo: From Classical Latin abstinentia; compare -y (suffix forming abstract nouns) and earlier abstinence, a doublet.

parole.significato: An institution for the study of higher learning; a college or a university; typically a private school.

parole.testo: From Middle English alphabete, borrowed from Classical Latin alphabētum, from Ancient Greek ἀλφάβητος (alphábētos), from ἄλφα (álpha) and βῆτα (bêta), the names of the first two letters of the Greek alphabet, Α (A) and Β (B), lowercase forms α and β. Borrowed from Classical Latin angulātus, from angulus (“angle”) + -ātus.
From Middle English angulatit, from Classical Latin angulātus + -ed. By surface analysis, angulate (verb) + -ed.

From Classical Latin ante-, use as prefix of ante (preposition); akin to Ancient Greek ἀντί (antí), Sanskrit अन्ति (anti), Gothic 𐌰𐌽𐌳- (and-) (only in compounds): compare answer, along, English ant-, ent- (in compounds). Doublet of anti-.

parole.significato: Any of several fibrous mineral forms of magnesium silicate, used for fireproofing, electrical insulation, building mate…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin asbestos, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἄσβεστος (ásbestos), from ἀ- (a-) + σβεστός (sbestós). Compare Middle English asbestus and Old French abestos.

parole.significato: A full brother: a brother born to the same mother and father, as distinguished from half brothers (uterine brothers), s…
parole.testo: From Middle English brother germain, equivalent to brother + german, after Anglo-Norman and Middle French frere germain and its etymon Classical Latin frāter germānus.

parole.significato: A police officer tasked with collecting evidence and information in order to solve a crime; an investigator.
parole.testo: The adjective is from Classical Latin dētēct-, past participial stem of dētegō (“to detect”), + -ive. By surface analysis, detect + -ive. From Classical Latin dictātōrius. By surface analysis, dictate + -ory.
Partly a learned borrowing from Classical Latin dulce, use as noun of neuter of dulcis, and partly from the adjective (etymology 1).

parole.significato: Someone who leaves a country to settle in a new country.
parole.testo: From Classical Latin ēmigrāns, present participle of ēmigrāre (“to emigrate”).

parole.significato: To make a journey, especially an excursion; to travel.
parole.testo: Probably partly from Classical Latin excurs-, past participial stem of excurrō, and partly from the noun.
From Classical Latin excursus. Doublet of excursus. In the “excursus” sense, some later examples in plural may show errors for excursuses.

parole.significato: A building or other place where manufacturing takes place.
parole.testo: Probably from factor + -y, although in noun sense 1 (“a place where manufacturing takes place”) apparently influenced strongly by association with Classical Latin fact-, the past participial stem of faciō (“to make”); compare manufactory and Latin factōrium (“an oil press”). From Middle English importune, inportune, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French importun and its etymon Classical Latin importūnus.

parole.significato: Having spots on the surface; spotted
parole.testo: From Classical Latin maculōsus. By surface analysis, macul(a) + -ose.
From Middle English maculose, maculous, from Classical Latin maculōsus. By surface analysis, macul(a) + -ous.
From Classical Latin medullāris. By surface analysis, medulla + -ary.

parole.significato: Of, from or pertaining to Memphis, Egypt.
parole.testo: From Middle English Memphyte, from Classical Latin Memphītis. By surface analysis, Memphis + -ite.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of Memphis, Egypt.
parole.testo: From Classical Latin Memphītēs, from Ancient Greek Μεμφῑ́της (Memphī́tēs).

parole.significato: To make noble; to ennoble; to exalt.
parole.testo: From Classical Latin nōbilitāt-, past participial stem of nōbilitō. By surface analysis, nobility + -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Take special note; used to add an aside or warning to a text.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Classical Latin notā bene (“note well”).
Learned borrowing from Classical Latin ōvi-, combining form (in e.g. ōviparus) of ōvum (“egg”).

parole.significato: Something perceived; the object of perception.
parole.testo: A learned borrowing, after concept, from Classical Latin perceptum (“a proposition, principle, general idea”), from the neuter of perceptus (“perceived”), the past participle of percipiō (“to perceive”); see perceive. Coined by the Scottish metaphysician Sir William Hamilton, 9th Baronet (1788–1856)
Learned borrowing from Classical Latin percept-, the past participial stem of percipiō (“to perceive”). In etymology 2 sense 2, perhaps independently from percept (“something perceived”).
Learned borrowing from Classical Latin profānāt-, the past participial stem of profānō. By surface analysis, profane + -ate.
From Classical Latin profānāt-, the past participial stem of profānō, + -ory. By surface analysis, profane + -atory.
From Middle English racionabilite, a learned borrowing from Classical Latin ratiōnābilitās. By surface analysis, ration(able) + -ability. Piecewise doublet of reasonability.
From Middle English racionable, a learned borrowing from Classical Latin ratiōnābilis. Doublet of reasonable.
From reposit or its etymon Classical Latin reposit-, past participial stem of repōnō, + -ory. Compare Medieval Latin repositōrius (“used for storage”).

parole.significato: The belief that the scientific method and the assumptions and research methods of the physical sciences are applicable…
parole.testo: From scient- (in either Classical Latin scientia or scientific) + -ism. Compare scientist.
From Classical Latin septēnārius; compare -ar. By surface analysis, septen- + -ar. Doublet of septenarius and septenary.

From Middle English septenarie, septenary, from Classical Latin septēnārius (“consisting of seven each”), from septēnus (“seven each; seven at a time”) + -ārius (whence the English suffix -ary). With use as noun compare septēnārius (“line of seven feet; unit of seven parts; period of seven years”).

parole.significato: A sister born of the same parents
parole.testo: From Middle English sister germain, equivalent to sister + german, after Anglo-Norman and Middle French suer germaine and its etymon Classical Latin germāna soror.

parole.significato: Expressing a wish that something will not happen, as in "May we never experience such hardship".

From Middle English violat, from Classical Latin violātus.
